revamp

ree-VAMP -- from 're-' (again) plus 'vamp,' the front part of a shoe. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To revamp is to give something a new and improved form.

The struggling airline hired new designers to revamp its outdated boarding process from the ground up.

Example

A run-down neighborhood diner is revamped from top to bottom -- cracked booths torn out, every wall repainted, the entire menu rewritten -- and reopens a month later almost unrecognizable.

That thorough rebuilding into something better is exactly what revamping delivers. Unlike 'repeat,' which keeps things the same, revamp changes and improves them.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

renovate: To renovate is to restore a building or room to good, updated condition -- the word stays close to physical spaces and repairs. To revamp is broader: you can revamp a menu, a website, a schedule, or a public image, redesigning it into an improved form.

modernize: To modernize is to update something specifically so it matches current times and technology. To revamp is any thorough makeover into a better form -- a revamp could even make a diner look charmingly old-fashioned, as long as it works better than before.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

neglect: to fail to take care of something

preserve: to keep something exactly as it was

Where it sits · how deep the makeover goes

refresh → revamp → overhaul

refresh vs. revamp: Refresh is much lighter than revamp -- refreshing a room or a menu means small touch-ups that leave the basic design alone, while a revamp rebuilds the whole look and workings into a new and better form.

overhaul vs. revamp: Overhaul can feel more intense than revamp: revamp often means giving something a fresh new look or approach, while overhaul suggests taking it apart down to its core and rebuilding it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-: again (Latin)

root — -vamp-: the front part of a shoe or boot (Old French (avant-pied, 'front of the foot'))

Put it together: Vamp originally named the front part of a shoe, from Old French avant-pied, 'front of the foot.' To revamp something first meant to patch up an old shoe's worn-out front -- the same 'front, before' idea survives in vanguard, the troops placed at the very front.

Use the root in a new word: vanguard: The small research team was the vanguard of a technology that would change the entire industry within a decade.

Word Building

Word Choice

Revamp often describes updating a product, program, image, or system to make it more effective or appealing, as in 'revamp the website.'
